html:
A scheme begun in 1997 to pump water from Lake Nasser, the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam, into canals in the Western Desert of Egypt, to create new farmland and towns.

Almost all Egyptians live on a narrow strip along the Nile and in its delta, and the population was growing fast. President Hosni Mubarak promised a second Nile valley in the desert that would one day hold millions of people. A giant pumping station lifts water into the Sheikh Zayed canal, named after the ruler of Abu Dhabi who helped pay for it.

Progress was far slower than promised. The land was hard to farm, the costs high, and few people moved there; large plots went to foreign investors. In recent years the government of President Sisi has revived the project with new farms. It raises the same question as Libya's Great Man-Made River: how far the desert can be made to bloom.
sum: A scheme begun in 1997 to pump water from Lake Nasser, the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam, into canals in the Western Desert of Egypt, to create new farmland and towns.
